note: At the end of Canto 2, Cato broke up the crowd listening to Casella's song and sent the souls running for the mountain.
The Italian word here, "ragion", can also mean justice. Many commentators read it that way: the mountain where God's justice searches the souls.

context: This canto shows the limits of the guide. Virgil doesn't know the way up, has to ask directions of the souls, and falls silent when he speaks of his own fate.

note: Virgil blames himself for standing idle to hear Casella sing. Cato's rebuke was aimed at the new souls, but the guide takes it to heart.
For Dante, as for Aristotle, a great-souled man does not run. Virgil's dignity returns when he slows to a walk.
The sun is still low in the east, just after sunrise, and the poets are walking west toward the mountain. Their shadows fall ahead of them.

quote: only darkness stretching ahead of me
note: Dante sees one shadow on the ground, his own, and for a moment thinks Virgil has left him. There was no sun in Hell, so this is the first time he notices that a shade casts no shadow. From here on, his shadow is what tells the souls he is alive.
It is early morning in Purgatory and evening in Italy, where Virgil's body lies. In Dante's Italian, Virgil calls it the body in which he used to cast a shadow.
Virgil died in 19 BC at Brindisi, the port on the heel of Italy, on his way home from Greece. The emperor Augustus had his remains carried to Naples, where a tomb is still shown as his.
In medieval astronomy the planets and stars were carried on nested spheres of transparent matter. Light passed through one sphere to the next without hindrance, as it now passes through Virgil.

quote: to suffer both burning cold and searing heat
note: The puzzle of the whole poem: how can a soul without flesh feel pain? Virgil says only that God makes it so and doesn't show how. A fuller answer is given in Purgatorio 25, where the poet Statius explains how the soul shapes itself a body of air.
The Trinity: one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. For medieval theology it was the chief example of a truth that reason can't reach unaided and that must be taken on faith.

quote: content with knowing that it is
note: A famous line. Dante's Italian says "be content with the quia", a Latin term from the philosophy schools. To know the quia is to know that a thing is so, from its effects, without knowing why. Human reason can see what God has done, not the causes behind it.

quote: Mary would not have needed to give birth
note: If human reason could have known everything, there would have been no need for Christ to come and reveal what it could not find out.

context: The great thinkers of Limbo wanted to know the highest truth. If reason alone could reach it, they would have reached it. Their longing is their only punishment, and Virgil shares it.

note: Virgil breaks off because the "many others" include himself.

The two ends of the Ligurian coast of northwest Italy: Lerici, on the Gulf of La Spezia, in the east, and La Turbie, above Monaco, in the west. Between them the mountains drop straight into the sea, and in Dante's day the roads were notoriously hard.
Dante, who has a body to haul up the rock. The shades weigh nothing.

The excommunicated: those who died cut off from the Church by its sentence but repented at the end. They defied authority in life. Here they move slowly and meekly, and must wait a long time before they may begin to climb.
Everyone on this mountain is sure of Heaven, however long the wait. Virgil greets them by the peace they will have and he will not.

quote: Time lost most troubles those who know its worth
note: One of the poem's proverbial lines. It is a lesson Virgil has just relearned from Cato.
A famous simile, drawn from life. It also fits these souls. They died outside the Church's flock, cast out by its shepherds. Now they are as mild and trusting as sheep.
The sun is now on Dante's left, so his shadow falls to the right, against the cliff. The souls have never seen a shadow here.
Dante could not have. Manfred was killed in February 1266, when Dante was less than a year old.
Chroniclers of the time also describe Manfred as fair-haired and handsome. Some readers hear an echo of the Bible's description of the young David.
A sword cut from the battle in which he died. The shades keep the look of their bodies, wounds included.

quote: a wound high on his chest
note: The second of his death wounds. Some commentators are reminded of the risen Christ showing his wounds to the apostle Thomas.

context: He smiles as he names himself. The Church had cursed him and thrown his body out of its grave, and the world thought him damned. Finding him here among the saved is the canto's great surprise.

note: Constance of Hauteville (1154–1198), heiress of the Norman kings of Sicily and wife of the emperor Henry VI. Dante meets her in Paradiso 3. Manfred names his grandmother, not his father: he was the illegitimate son of the emperor Frederick II, whom Dante puts in Hell among the heretics (Inferno 10).
Constance, named for her great-grandmother. She married King Peter III of Aragon and was still living in 1300.

quote: mother of Sicily's honor and Aragon's
note: In 1300 two of her sons were kings: James II of Aragon and Frederick of Sicily. The praise is a father's. Dante himself speaks poorly of both in Purgatorio 7.
Manfred died excommunicated, so everyone assumed he was in Hell. He wants his daughter to know otherwise, so that she will pray for him.
Dante lets Manfred admit it without saying what the sins were. The papal party accused him of loose living and of murdering members of his own family to get the crown. How much was true is not known.
The center of the canto: one moment of true repentance, even in the last breath, is enough. Dante will show the same in Canto 5.
The archbishop of Cosenza, in Calabria, usually identified as Bartolomeo Pignatelli. On the pope's orders he had Manfred's body dug up, since an excommunicate could not lie in the kingdom's soil.
Pope Clement IV (1265–1268), a Frenchman. He backed Charles of Anjou's conquest of Manfred's kingdom.
The page of Scripture that tells of God's mercy to those who turn to him. Manfred's point is that the bishop knew God's justice and forgot his mercy.
A town in southern Italy, northeast of Naples. Manfred was defeated and killed outside it on 26 February 1266.
Manfred could not be given a church burial. The story goes that he was buried at the foot of the bridge, and each soldier of the enemy army laid a stone on the grave, in respect for a brave man.
Usually identified as the Liri, or Garigliano, which marked the border between the Kingdom of Naples and the lands of the pope. The bones were dumped just beyond the border.
The rite for the excommunicated: no chanting and no light, the candles put out and carried upside down.
A bold claim. The Church's sentence can cut a person off from the sacraments, but not from God's love. Popes and bishops do not have the last word on a soul.

quote: as long as hope shows any green
note: As long as there is life. Green is the color of hope, and of a plant that isn't dead yet.

context: The excommunicated are the first of the groups kept waiting here, at the very foot of the mountain.

note: The figure is Dante's own, not Church teaching. For every year a soul stayed under the ban, it waits thirty here. Manfred has been dead thirty-four years.
The prayers of the living, if they come from a heart in God's grace, shorten the time. This is why soul after soul in Purgatory will ask Dante to carry word home.
